title: Streamed planets: 880 x 880 tiles
summary: Planet surfaces are now 880 x 880 tiles - ten times wider and a hundred times bigger than before - with Minoan villages scattered across them. To make that possible the surface is no longer built all at once: a worker thread generates the whole planet (terrain, village plans with levelled plots, causeways, the ground and map pictures) while you land, and the world is then made around you as you move - scenery in 16 x 16-tile chunks grown on worker threads and freed behind you (it grows back the same), buildings and citizens as you come near, and a path-finding grid that follows you and is rebuilt in parallel. Landing takes about 4 s without a single stalled frame, walking stays smooth, the minimap shows the land around you, and the planet map lets you set out for anywhere on the planet.

steps.title: From 88 x 88 to 880 x 880 tiles
steps.text: Planet surfaces were 88 tiles a side and built whole while you landed. Now they are 880 a side - 100 times the area, several minutes to cross on foot - so nothing can be built whole any more: the planet is generated in the background and made around you, piece by piece.

steps.title: The whole planet is planned on a worker thread
steps.text: While the landing animation plays, a worker thread generates the planet: terrain heights for all 774,400 tiles, the villages' plans with their plots levelled, causeways to islands, and the ground and map pictures as raw bytes. The main thread only waits a frame at a time, so the game never stalls; it then turns the bytes into textures.

~2 s of work - no frame over ~40 ms

steps.title: Villages all over the planet
steps.text: The planet is split into 110 x 110-tile regions; about every other one gets a village (sometimes with a palace). Next to the landing pad there is always a palace, a warehouse and a temple. Every building is at least 12 x 12 tiles, on a plot levelled for it: water, rock and crevasses under it and two tiles around are turned to dry ground, easing into the land beyond.

steps.title: Scenery streams in 16 x 16-tile chunks
steps.text: Trees, rocks, grass and flowers are grown per chunk of 16 x 16 tiles on worker threads, nearest first, and placed a few milliseconds per frame. The 5 x 5 chunks around you are kept full; chunks more than 4 away are freed. Each chunk's scenery is seeded by its position, so a chunk you come back to grows back exactly the same.

steps.title: Small pieces each frame
steps.text: Nothing big happens in one frame. Scenery placement has a 3 ms budget per frame. Buildings and citizens appear when you come within 64 tiles, one building per frame. Each chunk's trees sit under one holder node, so freeing a chunk is a single removal from the y-sorted scene instead of a thousand.

diagram.label: a building coming into view (within 64 tiles): one per frame

steps.title: A path grid that follows you
steps.text: Path-finding used one grid over the whole map; at 880 x 880 that would be 12 million points. Now the grid covers a 96 x 96-tile window around you, and is built again around you when you're 24 tiles off its centre. It's built on worker threads in three stages - walkable rows in parallel, edge checks in parallel, then the grid with its doorways - in 0.65 s instead of 3.2 s.

steps.title: Walking somewhere far away
steps.text: On the planet map (M) you can click anywhere on the planet. If it's outside the path grid's window, you set out toward it: each leg goes to the edge of the window, the window moves with you, and the next leg starts, until you arrive.

steps.title: Maps and saved layouts
steps.text: The corner minimap now shows the land around you (about 140 tiles); the planet map shows the whole planet with every village's buildings and zooms much further in. Both use the map picture made on the worker thread. Saving a layout in the level editor keeps every building and citizen - built yet or not - and only the scenery you placed by hand; the rest grows back by itself.

steps.title: Results
steps.text: Landing on a planet ten times wider takes about 3.5-4 s, and the game stays smooth the whole time. Walking at four times normal speed across the planet, the worst frame was 46 ms (67 ms with rendering, when a village appears). All 58 automated tests pass, including a new test of the streamed planet.

Each chunk's scenery is worked out on a worker thread...
